docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet covers the design, implementation, and component selection for the MQTT subsystem. My subsystem is responsible for implementing a two-way wireless communication between my board (via an ESP32 microcontroller) and an external server (MQTT Explorer) via MQTT network protocol.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
Our team is building an autonomous rover that uses a daisy-chained UART communication network to connect multiple subsystems together. Each team member was responsible for one subsystem. My board is in the middle of the daisy chain and passes down some commands to the next board in the chain, and takes some data and sends it to the MQTT Explorer server.

Link to my team report: Team Report

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text: I was responsible for designing and implementing an MQTT subsystem. This mainly includes: * Designing a functional two-way communication system between different boards using UART. * Designing a functional two-way wireless communication system between my board and the internet using MQTT.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text: Essentially, I designed the MQTT subsystem around making sure the ESP32 would run stable and reliably while handling wireless communication. Since the ESP32 already has built-in Wi-Fi and supports MQTT, I used it as the main controller and focused on supporting it properly with a solid power setup. Since it requires 3.3V, I used an LM2575-3.3V voltage regulator to make sure it always gets a steady supply, and then used capacitors and inductors to smooth out noise and handle any sudden current spikes, and then there are the enable and boot buttons of course. My subsystem does not have any sensors/actuators because I was responsible for the MQTT.

docs.title: Selected Component
docs.text: LM2575D2T-3.3WU-TR

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text: I chose the LM2575D2T-3.3WU-TR because it comes in a smaller SOT-23 package and can supply up to 1 A, giving us more current headroom in a compact design. It also includes an ON/OFF pin, which gives us better control over power management in the circuit. It is also a switching regulator.

docs.title: Review of Module's Sucess
docs.text:
I succeeded in connecting the ESP32 to MQTT Explorer and having commands sent both ways (from the board to MQTT explorer and vice versa).

I also succeeded in receiving and sending data via RX and TX by using the UART communication protocol.

docs.title: Module Startup
docs.text: Basically, the main issue I had with starting up the module was that I did not have the proper firmware installed. I just wish I had known that, and it would have saved me a few hours of troubleshooting.

docs.title: Lessons Learned
docs.text: From working on this project, I learned a lot about both the design and implementation of a PCB system. One of the biggest takeaways was how important it is to plan everything out before starting the schematic and layout, including choosing the right components and understanding their datasheets. I learned how to design a stable power system using a 3.3V regulator and proper decoupling capacitors, and also how important PCB layout decisions are, especially things like grounding, component placement, and making sure to choose the correct trace widths depending on the current. I also learned how to create and double check custom footprints, after making a mistake with a push button that caused it to always be connected. On the assembly side, I learned how to use solder paste and a heat gun for surface-mount components. That made soldering and working with surface-mount components a lot easier than whan I tried to solder them the standard way. I also gained experience flashing firmware onto an ESP32 and using MQTT to send and receive data. Throughout the project, I improved my debugging skills by dealing with both hardware and software issues, and I learned that testing smaller parts of the system step by step is much more effective than trying to build everything at once. Finally, I learned how to apply feedback from design reviews and how even small design mistakes can have a big impact on the final system.

docs.title: Recommendations for Future Students
docs.text:
1. Start your design early and try not to procrastinate, because waiting for the board to get here takes time to get here in and of itself.
  2. Test your system in smaller sections instead of trying to get everything working at once. It makes debugging much easier.
  3. Try to get experience with using solder paste and heatguns. It makes soldering surface-mount components a lot easier.
  4. Consider making surface-mount pads slightly wider than the width of the component's terminals. That can also make soldering easier.
  5. Pay close attention to PCB layout, including trace widths, grounding, and component placement, because these directly affect performance.

docs.title: Microcontroller Selection
docs.text:
Selected microcontroller: ESP-32

Rationale:

  • Built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth – The ESP32 has integrated 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and Bluetooth (Classic + BLE), so you don’t need extra communication modules, which reduces cost and board space.

  • Powerful and cost-effective – It has a dual-core processor, plenty of GPIOs, ADCs, PWM, SPI, I²C, etc., at a relatively low price.

  • Strong ecosystem and support – It’s widely used, has a lot of documentation documentation, and a large community, making work with it faster and easier.

  • Good for IoT applications – It supports secure communication (WPA2, TLS, encryption), making it suitable for connected and cloud-based systems.

docs.title: Hardware 2.0
docs.text: If I were to do my PCB over again to try and improve it, a few things come to mind right away. First of all, perhaps the most obvious improvement I would make is having all my components be surface-mount. That was what I had intended originally, but unfortunately, some of the surface-mount components would not have been able to come in time, so I had to settle for through-hole components instead. Second, I would check my footprints to make sure that they are all designed properly. The main issue that I had with footprints is the footprint for my buttons. When I first made the footprint, I accidentally numbered the pins in the footprint differently from how the pins were numbered in the schematic. Because of that, my footprint ended up connecting all four of the button’s pins regardless of whether the button was pressed or not. Because of that, I had to cut off two of the legs of my button and use only its remaining two legs in order to make it actually work like a button. So, again, I would do a better job of checking and designing my footprints. Third, and also related to the topic of footprints: I would design the pads to be a little wider (specifically, the surface-mount pads). A prominent issue that I faced a lot was that my surface-mount pads kept coming off when I tried to solder the component to it. And aside from that, even when the pads did not come off, it was still often difficult to solder the component onto the pad because the size of the pad was just enough to get the component soldered onto it. Now that I have visualized and experienced just how small these surface-mount pads really are, I would take that into consideration if I were to redesign the PCB. Finally, (this issue is not really a major hardware issue but more of a small design issue), I would redesign the PCB so that all of the component reference designators would be closer to the component itself. When I was designing the PCB in KiCAD, I did not know the difference between the silkscreen layer and the fabrication layer, and I did not know that the fabrication layer will not get printed onto the final PCB. Because of that, I had both of them on and the fabrication layer text pushed the silkscreen layer text up, which made it appear farther from the components on my PCB than it should have. Aside from that, everything did more-or-less work.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
I used it to determine whether my components like the ESP32 and the LEDs will have enough voltage/current to operate. And I came to the conclusion that they would, as the ESP32 does not take up too much power.

Also, choosing a switching regulator was a good choice because a linear regulator wastes a lot more voltage through heat than a switching one does.
